title: MobilePA-Bench: Phone Agents in a Live Sandbox
hook: GUI benchmarks test tapping; function-call benchmarks test string matching. This one runs a real phone sandbox with live app databases — and frontier models get brittle fast.
key_points: Existing mobile agent benchmarks split into GUI screen manipulation and offline API matching; neither tests long-horizon planning under real runtime constraints.
MobilePA-Bench runs an executable sandbox with live application databases that return structured feedback.
It spans 13 functional domains and 212 realistic mobile tools.
Beyond basic tool use it scores three dimensions: sub-agent collaboration, memory usage, and skill usage.
Frontier LLMs degrade sharply under strict tool ordering, permission limits, and unexpected runtime errors.
content_html: Phones are becoming the main venue for personal agents, which makes evaluating them on a phone — not on a transcript of one — the interesting problem. Zhu and colleagues argue existing benchmarks fall into two camps with complementary blind spots: GUI benchmarks measure screen manipulation and ignore background tool use and planning, while static function-calling benchmarks compare against offline API traces that have nothing to do with runtime reality.
extra_html:
A stateful sandbox

MobilePA-Bench runs agents against an executable sandbox with live application databases that return structured feedback, covering 13 functional domains and 212 realistic mobile tools. Because the state persists, an agent's earlier mistakes actually cost it later. On top of straightforward tool use, the benchmark grades a central planner on three harder abilities: decomposing a task and delegating to specialized sub-agents, recalling stored memories and user preferences to resolve implicit requests, and invoking pre-packaged composite skills instead of replanning from scratch.

What it finds

Current frontier models are not reliable here. The authors report sharp drops when tools must be called in a strict order, when permissions are restricted, and when the runtime throws unexpected errors — the ordinary conditions of a real device. The sandbox doubles as an environment for agentic RL, which is arguably its longer-term contribution.
